• Authorizes a $5 million Development Loan to Campbell Cove, Ltd. (Vestcor) for construction of a 240-unit apartment community to be located at 11000 Beach Blvd.
• All units will be restricted for those at or below 60% AMI
• The Development Loan will have a 20-year term with 1% interest per year with interest-only payments through maturity and a balloon principal payment at the end of the term
• The loan can be repaid in full or in part at any time with no penalty
• The loan will become due and payable to the City if the project no longer qualifies as affordable housing during the term of the loan
• The Developer is required to provide annual audits and if the General Partner or affiliates of the General Partner collectively receive distributions and/or loan interest payments in excess of $500,000 in any year, the excess will be paid to the City and used to reduce the principal balance of the loan
• Waives the Public Investment Policy to authorize a Development Loan, which is not an authorized incentive under the policy

Mr. Everett asked the panel how they would define the difference between a capital project and asset-based investments. Daryl Joseph of the Parks Department said his department classifies items by cost, noting that anything over $100,000 is usually considered a capital investment. He said the purchase of equipment, like furniture, would be considered an asset-based investment. Nina Sickler of the Public Works Department said they consider the useful life of something when classifying it as either a capital or asset-based investment, noting that a capital investment will be safe and usable for 30 or more years. Robert Waremburg from the Procurement Division said that, with capital investments, consideration should be given to whether they entail construction or professional design services, as there are laws and procedures that must be followed when selecting architects and engineers.

CM Arias asked if projects funded must be opened to public use. Mr. Waremburg said it depended on whether the City owns the property. Mr. Joseph said that any dollars put into a facility by the City, regardless of ownership, would be associated with public use. He added that, with privately owned facilities, a joint-use agreement may be required once City funds are accepted.

They are adjacent to each other and include the City’s downtown along West Bay Drive and the Clearwater-Largo Road corridor. Capital improvements and redevelopment activities in the WBD-CRD are primarily funded through Tax Increment Financing (TIF) revenues. The TIF does not require that properties located in the WBD-CRD pay additional property taxes. Rather, a portion of the annual City and County taxes collected in the redevelopment area are transferred to the CRA as a trust fund to be used for redevelopment activities. There is currently no TIF funding in place for the CLR-CRD. Largo's TIF District for the WBD-CRD was established in 2000 and is used to leverage public funds to promote private sector activity, redevelopment and infrastructure projects in accordance with the redevelopment plan. Discussion Land and construction costs have continued to escalate this past year continuing to make it difficult for people to purchase their first home and for developers to build affordable housing. During this same period, there has been a significant increase in short-term rental properties, particularly in single-family neighborhoods, which has also restricted the available housing stock for first-time homebuyers. Funding is limited for the construction of affordable housing as well as for public services to provide the support system to lift households out of poverty and help them become self-sustaining. Through public and private partnerships, the City will continue to strive to leverage the City's grant funding to expand the reach of programs and services provided to the Largo community. Incentives such as density bonuses can also help offset the per-unit cost for construction.

FSU agrees to use its best efforts to secure funding, through grants, donations, appropriations and other available funding sources to either FSU or TMH, to support improvements to the City Assets and related healthcare services. This long-term investment, which includes the contributions to citizens and the short-term investments described above, is expected to exceed $1.7 billion over the 30 years following the transfer of the City Assets. These funds are intended to support the development of new clinical spaces, laboratory and research facilities, expanded clinical research programs, additional academic faculty, and upgrades to the facilities and physical plant, all foundational elements of building a leading academic health center anchored by the City Assets. Such efforts and funding resources will create new jobs, fund the purchase of new equipment, and most importantly, improve healthcare and facilitate innovative medical treatments that will benefit the citizens of Tallahassee and hospital patients.
